content: 1. The effectiveness of clopidogrel may be reduced by drugs that inhibit the CYP2C19 enzyme. Clopidogrel's antiplatelet activity is entirely dependent on its active metabolite, which is partially metabolized by CYP2C19. Pantoprazole co-administration with clopidogrel does not have a clinically significant effect on the exposure to clopidogrel's active metabolite, and no dose adjustment of clopidogrel is required. 2. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of crizotinib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Drugs that elevate gastric pH may reduce the solubility and bioavailability of crizotinib. However, no formal studies have been conducted to confirm this. 3. Pantoprazole and cyclosporine may increase each other's toxicity through mechanisms not fully understood. Prolonged use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like pantoprazole can cause hypomagnesemia, and this risk is further increased when used with other drugs that have similar effects. 4. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of dabrafenib by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Drugs that alter upper gastrointestinal tract pH, such as PPIs, H2-blockers, and antacids, may reduce dabrafenib solubility and bioavailability. 5. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of diazepam (both buccal and intranasal forms) by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism. Strong or moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors may decrease the rate of diazepam elimination, increasing the risk of adverse reactions. 6. Pantoprazole increases the toxicity of digoxin by mechanisms not fully understood. Prolonged use of PPIs may cause hypomagnesemia, which increases the risk of digoxin toxicity. 7. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of duvelisib by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Co-administration of duvelisib, a BCRP substrate, with a BCRP transport inhibitor may increase duvelisib levels or effects. 8. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of ferrous salts (e.g., ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, ferrous sulfate) and ferric compounds (e.g., ferric gluconate, ferric maltol) by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. 9. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of fexinidazole by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism. 10. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of finerenone by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor serum potassium during initiation and dosage adjustment of either finerenone or weak CYP3A4 inhibitors, and adjust finerenone dosage as needed. 11. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of fosamprenavir by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. 12. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir by decreasing metabolism. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir may also increase plasma concentrations of P-gp and BCRP substrates. 13. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of iron dextran complex and iron sucrose by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. 14. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of isavuconazonium sulfate by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. 15. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of itraconazole by increasing gastric pH. For patients using the Sporanox brand of itraconazole (capsules or solution), administer PPIs at least 2 hours before or after itraconazole. Use of Sporanox oral solution or administration of itraconazole with an acidic beverage (e.g., cola) may minimize the significance of this interaction. 16. Pantoprazole decreases the levels of ledipasvir/sofosbuvir by increasing gastric pH. Ledipasvir solubility decreases as pH increases. Proton pump inhibitor doses comparable to omeprazole <20 mg can be administered simultaneously with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir under fasted conditions. 17. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of methotrexate by decreasing renal clearance. There is an increased risk of toxicity with higher doses of methotrexate. 18. Pantoprazole decreases the effects of methylphenidate by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Since the characteristics of methylphenidate extended-release capsules (Ritalin LA) are pH-dependent, co-administration of antacids or acid suppressants could alter the release of methylphenidate. 19. Pantoprazole increases the toxicity of theophylline by mechanisms not fully understood. Prolonged use of PPIs can cause hypochlorhydria, which may alter intestinal motility and increase the risk of toxicity. 20. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of mycophenolate by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies to the prodrug mycophenolate mofetil conversion to active mycophenolic acid. Enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium formulation is less sensitive to this interaction. 21. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of tacrolimus by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism. Concomitant administration may increase tacrolimus whole blood concentrations, particularly in intermediate or poor metabolizers of CYP2C19. 22. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of vismodegib by increasing gastric pH. Drugs that increase gastric pH alter vismodegib solubility and reduce bioavailability, though the effect on efficacy is unknown. 23. Pantoprazole increases the levels or effects of voriconazole by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C19 metabolism and hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. 24. Pantoprazole decreases the levels or effects of cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) by reducing gastric acidity, which is necessary for vitamin B12 absorption.
